lessons.title: Skeleton guard + hue recover: Arc palette up, Trialta/suite down

Arc import/plate best-engine rose ~0.56-0.63 to ~0.69-0.72 via palette (0.19-0.27 to 0.74-1.00) but ink_iou stayed ~0.25-0.31 — JPEG geometry ceiling, not a threshold. lessons.title: Skeleton + hue lock raise Arc palette, not suite 0.90
lessons.lesson: Three structural passes in logo_raster_finish / logo_vectorize: (1) medial-axis centerline computed on raw contrast BEFORE knockout/halo, those passes cannot punch skeleton pixels; (2) hue-consistent recover projects 8-25 percent sat boundary pixels onto the observed HSV cluster median within +/-25 deg (no invented hues); (3) thin vtracer path quantizes to 2-4 colors, spline/filter_speckle=1/color_precision=8/layer_difference=16, then stamps dropped centerline. Arc palette jumped (import vectorize 0.19 to 0.94) but ink_iou stayed ~0.25-0.31 so composite only reached 0.66-0.72. Hue-consistent recover is thin-only; a single hue anchor on multi-fill lockups is a regression.

lessons.title: The improve wall was the scoreboard: composite cannot score a perfect restoration
lessons.lesson: Feeding a clean reference back in AS ITS OWN restoration scores 0.9331 (swift_orange), 0.9500 (swift_orange_solid), 0.9225 (gcm) — not 1.0. composite's edge term is 0.10*min(eer,2.0)/2.0, which only pays out in full at TWICE the reference's edge energy; an exact copy has eer=1.0 and collects half. alpha_clean and palette_fidelity are absolute and the references do not score 1.0 on themselves. So 0.9269 on the Swift anchor was 0.0062 from a byte-identical copy, and the 0.97-0.99 target was unreachable by anything faithful — it requires eer>=2.0, i.e. deliberate ringing. Worse, the metric INVERTS ranking: swift_orange__blur_crush__vectorize scores legacy 0.9312 at eer=2.22 (visibly over-sharpened) while downscale_jpeg__vectorize scores legacy 0.9179 at eer=0.885 (faithful). Tuning to maximize composite selects for artifacts. Added composite_v2 (identity == 1.0 exactly, symmetric edge term) alongside; legacy composite left byte-identical and re-verified with zero drift across 54 rows.
lessons.do_not_regress: Swift vectorize mean 0.9269 on legacy composite; legacy composite must stay byte-identical

lessons.title: Raster-fidelity scoring is the wrong target; two brand SVGs are wrapped bitmaps
lessons.lesson: qa_logos/synthetic/clean/swift_orange.png has exactly two alpha values (0 and 255) and ZERO anti-aliased pixels — the reference is hard-edged with jaggies baked in, so IoU against it rewards reproducing the staircase. The goal is the artwork the raster is a degraded rendering OF, not a copy of it. Separately: assets/brand/swift_supply_logo_orange.svg and swift_supply_logo_orange_solid.svg contain NO vector geometry at all — they are base64 PNGs inside an <svg><image> wrapper (36708 and 159063 bytes of PNG). Any 'true-ink IoU 1.0000' measured on them is a bitmap scored against itself and means nothing. Only swift_supply_logo_document.svg (8992 anchors, 114.8/1k) and swift_supply_logo_white.svg (11614 anchors, 307.5/1k) have real paths, and both are dense raster traces. Added tools/logo_vectorizer/ideality.py: a reference-free score (anchor economy, straightness, curvature smoothness, staircase detection) calibrated against the one genuinely hand-built vector in the repo, briysce_wordmark_paper.svg at 57 anchors/1k => 0.9246.
lessons.do_not_regress: never quote fidelity from an <image>-wrapped SVG as vector quality

lessons.title: Establish intent by recognition, not inference: glyph > shape > residual
lessons.lesson: Ranked evidence beats statistics. (1) Run-level font ID: group elements by baseline/cap-height, pick the ONE font maximizing agreement across the run, then emit the font's own outline. Positive control 12/12 correct (font AND every character) for Oswald-Bold SUPPLY, Montserrat-Bold SWIFT, LiberationSans-Bold CARGO down to 0.18x scale + JPEG q40. On a degraded SUPPLY this cut anchors 149.6/1k -> 2.7/1k AND raised IoU vs the TRUE original 0.9479 -> 0.9776 — recognition beats tracing on BOTH quality and accuracy. Glyph must outrank generic polygon fit or an L/I gets claimed as a polygon and the real curves are lost. Placement must be refined by local offset/scale search against the element mask; naive bbox mapping lost ~0.5-3% IoU. (2) Shape vocabulary (circle/ellipse/rect/rotated-rect/regular-polygon/rounded-rect/polygon), most-constrained-wins by DOF. (3) Residual character only as last resort.
lessons.do_not_regress: glyph match must outrank generic polygon; placement refinement must stay on

lessons.title: Three metric traps: fixed coverage gates, side-length residuals, and equal sides without equal angles
lessons.lesson: All three produced wrong answers before being caught. (a) A fixed coverage threshold (0.972) is size-blind: a 44px circle tops out at 0.938 no matter how perfect the fit, because its 1px rim is ~6% of its area. Gate against the achievable ceiling 1-(perimeter*0.5*pixel/area) instead, or every small shape is rejected — exactly the low-res case that matters most. (b) Residual must mean the same thing for every primitive (mean boundary distance in px). Using side-length spread for polygons read ~15 on a clean large triangle and wrongly rejected it. (c) Regular polygon needs equal TURN ANGLES as well as equal sides: a kite has sides std/mean 0.018 (passes) but turn-angle std 6.72deg, and was falsely called regular. Also: never fall back to 'accept the best candidate anyway' when nothing passes the gate — inventing regularity that was not there is worse than tracing honestly.
lessons.do_not_regress: size-aware coverage floor; unified boundary residual; angle check on regular polygons

lessons.title: Damage metrics must be chosen empirically; most candidates invert on flat artwork
lessons.lesson: First cut of flaw_analysis scored the CLEAN anchor as more damaged (0.476) than blur_crush (0.306) — the same failure it accuses BRISQUE of. Three of five measures invert on flat art: posterization (flat brand art legitimately has 2-3 colours), staircase (clean anchors are hard-alpha renders so 100% of steps are on the pixel grid), and spectral cutoff (JPEG noise ADDS high-frequency energy, so damage reads as MORE resolution). Tested candidates against known severity across every slug and kept only ink_speckle (share of ink components <64px): monotonic everywhere — swift_orange 0.00/0.71/0.91, gcm 0.00/0.80/0.96, propak 0.04/0.80/0.93, trialta 0.00/0.71/0.95. Rejected hf_noise (gcm clean 0.377 > degraded 0.268), contour roughness, chroma variance, and BRISQUE (clean 171.46 vs degraded 93.68/96.88 — ranks pristine worst, needs 3 shims to even run). Known asymmetry: speckle is strong positive evidence but its absence proves little; a clean 0.18x/q40 rescale still reports ~0.10. Score only ever RAISES correction strength from a safe baseline, so a false low is a missed opportunity, not a regression.
lessons.do_not_regress: never wire BRISQUE into the degradation score; validate any new damage metric for monotonicity across all slugs first

lessons.title: RANSAC consensus over least-squares for damaged primitives; corpus size gates font ID
lessons.lesson: A mean-radius circle fit is least-squares so every outlier pulls it — wrong estimator for damaged artwork. RANSAC (pyransac3d, 2D lifted to z=0) finds the circle the largest agreeing subset supports and treats damage as outliers. A/B: chunk bitten out 4.34px/7.32px centre/radius error -> 1.50/0.45; ragged bled edge 5.30/0.64 -> 1.57/1.04; IDENTICAL on clean input, so no regression. Keep the robust fit only when it beats the least-squares coverage. Separately: font ID is bounded by corpus, not by matcher tuning. Swift SUPPLY (a Eurostile/Microgramma-like square face) scored 0.608 against 103 system fonts and 0.851 against 458 after pulling Google Fonts via the css2 API — still below the 0.86 run threshold, so it correctly declines. Note Google content-negotiates format from User-Agent: a BROWSER UA gets WOFF (PIL cannot open it), an unrecognized UA gets plain TTF.
lessons.do_not_regress: RANSAC must not change clean-input fits; font_fetch must not send a browser UA

lessons.title: Simplify-then-fit beats tracing on clean bold artwork, and loses everywhere else
lessons.lesson: potrace follows the pixel boundary faithfully, which means faithfully reproducing stair-steps: the Swift lockup traced to 28,643 anchors at 196.9 per 1k contour against 57 for the hand-built briysce wordmark. Replacing the tracer with RDP simplify -> Chaikin -> Catmull-Rom (smooth.py, which already existed and named SWIFT in its docstring but was never called by idealize) gives ~2,600 anchors at ~32/1k and ideality 0.5985 -> 0.8691 on swift_orange, 0.6277 -> 0.8502 on swift_orange_solid. Rendered at 3x the S becomes one continuous sweep where the source and potrace are both visibly staircased. BUT it wins only 1-2 cases in 17: on arc/gcm/propak (all <720px) it LOSES 0.08-0.11 because corner-cutting adds points on short contours RDP barely reduced, and on every degraded input it is far worse (0.55-0.70 vs potrace 0.75-0.84) because RDP+Chaikin on a noisy contour makes mush. So build both and keep the measured winner, guarded by shape agreement with a 0.06 budget.
lessons.do_not_regress: never declare one fitter the winner from the Swift result alone; keep the build-both-and-measure chooser

lessons.title: Simplification tolerance must never approach the feature size
lessons.lesson: RDP epsilon in smooth.py is a fraction of PERIMETER, which is the wrong yardstick for a long thin shape. The Swift bars are 2981x93, so a perimeter-based epsilon lands near 4% of their height; with the corner-cutting pass on top the parallel edges converge and the bar leaves as a tapered wedge. Shape agreement caught it (0.893 vs potrace 0.9957) and the chooser refused the candidate, costing a real +0.22 ideality win until the cause was found. Fix: cap epsilon at 2% of each contour's own thinnest bounding dimension (RDP_THIN_FRACTION). swift_orange_solid smooth IoU then went 0.893 -> 0.9625 and the chooser accepted it. Related: the same bars ARE rect-snapped in swift_orange (2981x91) but not in swift_orange_solid (2981x93) because the letters touch them there and coverage drops below the strict gate — worth fixing separately so bars never reach the fitter at all. Also note potrace scored 0.996 raster agreement on that logo with visibly jagged edges: high raster agreement and good craftsmanship are different things.
lessons.do_not_regress: RDP epsilon capped against contour thinnest dimension; bars must keep parallel edges

lessons.title: A bounding fit is the wrong estimator for a shape that carries damage
lessons.lesson: cv2.minAreaRect must enclose every boundary pixel, so a handful of antialiasing crumbs sets the size AND the angle of the whole rectangle. Three stray pixels out of 268,100 stretched the solid Swift top bar from 2980x89 to 2980x91 down its entire length (coverage 0.9993 -> 0.9776, under the gate, bar refused and traced as a curve); on a shorter 300px bar the same three crumbs also tilted it 0.28 degrees, which smears the edges across 1.5px and defeats any trim taken in that frame. Fix both with consensus estimates -- extents from quantiles of the boundary, orientation from the element's own second moments -- and let rendered coverage pick among them with the bounding fit still in the running, so a genuine rectangle cannot be talked out of its real size. Same argument fit_circle already made for RANSAC over least squares.
lessons.do_not_regress: Trim fractions do not scale down: 0.4% of a 6150-point outline sheds 3 crumbs, but 0.4% of a 680-point outline is fewer points than those crumbs contribute and the trim silently no-ops. Try a ladder of trims and let coverage choose.

lessons.title: Clearing the coverage floor is not the same as fitting
lessons.lesson: best_fit ranked candidates by degrees of freedom on the principle that the more constrained shape is the stronger claim about intent -- but that principle is stated as 'when both fit within tolerance', and the code read it as 'both cleared the coverage floor'. The floor is a MINIMUM and relaxes to 0.80 on small elements, so a rect covering 0.8000 outranked a polygon covering 0.9728, and a rect covering 0.9611 outranked a polygon that fitted exactly. Gate the dof preference on the freer shape failing to remove most of the tighter one's leftover error, measured as a FRACTION of that leftover so the test means the same thing at every element size, and only while there is material error left -- otherwise it turns hair-trigger as coverage approaches 1 and noise decides in the other direction.
lessons.do_not_regress: A relative-error criterion is meaningless once the leftover error is tiny; require the constrained shape to be leaving at least MATERIAL_ERROR uncovered before asking the question at all.

lessons.title: A score is only a score next to the settings that produced it
lessons.lesson: The improve loop recorded composite scores but nothing about the configuration behind them. Re-running with --engines baseline,vectorize --min-height 3000 and comparing against a history of --engines baseline,esrgan,vectorize --min-height 1200 runs showed Swift vectorize anchors at 0.9234 vs 0.9269 and read as a 0.0035 regression in the default path. It was not one: min_height feeds the Lanczos target, the SVG rasterize width and the scale the metrics are measured at, and the engine set changes anchor_mean_composite because that mean averages across engines. Nothing in the log said so, so the two runs looked comparable. min_height and the engine list are now recorded on every row and in the summary.
lessons.do_not_regress: Never compare improve-loop runs without checking min_height and engines match; the loop's --min-height default is 1200 and the historical anchor baseline (vectorize Swift = 0.9269 composite / 0.9356 v2) was measured there.
